title: The Window · 13
paragraphs: He had been to Amsterdam, Mr. Bankes was telling Lily Briscoe as they walked across the lawn. He’d seen the Rembrandts. He’d been to Madrid. Unluckily it was Good Friday, and the Prado was closed. He’d been to Rome. Had Miss Briscoe never been to Rome? Oh, she ought to— It would be a marvelous experience for her—the Sistine Chapel; Michelangelo; and Padua, with its Giottos. For years his wife’s health had been poor, so their sightseeing had been done on a modest scale.

She had been to Brussels; she had been to Paris, though only on a quick trip to visit a sick aunt. She had been to Dresden; there were masses of pictures she’d never seen; but perhaps, Lily Briscoe reflected, it was better not to see pictures: all they did was make you hopelessly dissatisfied with your own work. Mr. Bankes felt you could take that view too far. We can’t all be Titians and we can’t all be Darwins, he said; yet he doubted whether there could be any Darwin or Titian without humble people like ourselves. Lily wanted to pay him a compliment; you’re not humble, Mr. Bankes, she would have liked to say. But he didn’t want compliments (most men do, she thought), and a little ashamed of the impulse, she kept quiet while he remarked that perhaps what he’d said didn’t apply to pictures. At any rate, said Lily, dashing off her small insincerity, she would always keep on painting, because it interested her. Yes, Mr. Bankes said, he was sure of that. As they came to the end of the lawn he was asking whether she found it hard to find subjects in London, when they turned and saw the Ramsays. So that is marriage, Lily thought: a man and a woman watching a girl throw a ball. That is what Mrs. Ramsay was trying to tell me the other night, she thought. For Mrs. Ramsay had on a green shawl, and the two stood close together, watching Prue and Jasper throw catches. And suddenly the meaning that comes down on people for no reason at all—as they’re stepping out of the Underground, perhaps, or ringing a doorbell—and makes them symbolic, makes them representative, came down on these two, and turned them, standing and gazing in the dusk, into the symbols of marriage, husband and wife. Then, after an instant, the symbolic outline that rose above the real figures sank again, and as Lily and Mr. Bankes came up to them they were simply Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay watching the children throw catches. Yet for a moment still—though Mrs. Ramsay greeted them with her usual smile (oh, she thinks we’re going to get married, Lily thought) and said, “I’ve triumphed tonight,” meaning that for once Mr. Bankes had agreed to have dinner with them rather than hurrying back to his lodgings, where his manservant cooked vegetables the proper way—still, for a single moment, there was a feeling of things blown apart, of space, of irresponsibility, as the ball soared up, and their eyes followed it and lost it and found the one star and the draped branches. In the fading light they all looked sharp-edged and unearthly and set apart by great distances. Then, dashing backward across the huge space (for solidity seemed to have vanished completely), Prue ran full tilt into them and brilliantly caught the ball high up in her left hand; and her mother said, “Aren’t they back yet?” and at that the spell broke. Now Mr. Ramsay felt free to laugh out loud at Hume, who had got stuck in a bog and was rescued by an old woman on condition that he said the Lord’s Prayer; and chuckling to himself, he wandered off to his study.
